title: Fire Damage Insurance Claim Help: A Galveston House Fire Guide
description: Fire damage insurance claim help for Galveston homeowners: the first 72 hours, documenting losses, ALE, contents, and how to avoid a low fire settlement.
html:
If your Galveston home has just been through a fire, you are dealing with two emergencies at once: getting your family safe and housed, and protecting the insurance claim that will pay to rebuild. This guide gives you practical fire damage insurance claim help in the order you actually need it, from the first phone call to the final settlement, written for homeowners on Galveston Island and across Galveston County.

Good fire damage insurance claim help starts with a plan, because the decisions you make in the first week can affect the claim for months. Nothing here replaces reading your own policy. Every homeowners policy is different, and the wording of yours controls what is covered. But the steps below apply to almost every residential fire claim in Texas, and following them early prevents the most common and expensive mistakes.

The First 72 Hours After a House Fire

What you do in the first few days sets the tone for the whole claim. Insurers expect you to act reasonably to protect the property and to give prompt notice. Here is a short checklist:

  1. Get the fire report. Ask the Galveston Fire Department (or your local county department) how to request the incident report. Your insurer will ask for it, and it records the cause and origin as the responding officers saw it.
  2. Report the claim right away. Call your carrier or agent, write down the claim number, and note the name of everyone you speak with and the date.
  3. Secure the property. Board up openings, tarp the roof, and shut off utilities if they are not already off. Most policies require you to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage. Keep every receipt for board-up, tarping, fencing and security.
  4. Ask about Additional Living Expense (ALE). If the home is not livable, your policy likely includes Loss of Use coverage for hotel, rental and increased food costs. Ask what the limit is and how they want receipts submitted.
  5. Do not throw anything away yet. Burned furniture, clothing and electronics are evidence. Photograph them before any disposal, and ask the adjuster in writing before discarding damaged items.

Document Everything Before Cleanup Starts

The single biggest factor in a fair fire settlement is documentation. Adjusters pay for what can be shown. Before mitigation crews start tearing out drywall, walk the property (only when the fire department says it is safe) and record:

  • Wide video of every room, then close-up photos of each wall, ceiling, floor and fixture.
  • Soot patterns on ceilings, inside cabinets, closets and HVAC registers in rooms that did not burn. Smoke travels well beyond the fire room, and those areas are frequently underpaid.
  • The exterior: siding, soffits, roof, windows and any heat damage to neighboring structures such as fences or detached garages.
  • Model and serial numbers on appliances, HVAC equipment and water heaters.

Keep a simple claim diary. Write down every call, visit and promise with the date. When a dispute arises months later, a dated log is far more persuasive than memory.

Understanding What Your Fire Policy Covers

A typical Texas homeowners policy splits a fire loss into several coverages. Knowing them helps you make sure nothing is left on the table:

  • Dwelling (Coverage A): the structure itself, including framing, roofing, electrical, plumbing, built-in cabinets and flooring.
  • Other Structures (Coverage B): detached garages, sheds, fences and similar structures.
  • Personal Property (Coverage C): furniture, clothing, electronics, kitchen items and other belongings.
  • Loss of Use (Coverage D): Additional Living Expense while you cannot live in the home.
  • Debris removal and code upgrade coverage: often a separate percentage or endorsement. Rebuilding in Galveston may trigger current building code requirements, especially for older homes, so check whether you have ordinance or law coverage. Our Galveston local code page explains the local requirements that commonly come up.

Also check whether your policy pays replacement cost or actual cash value. Many replacement cost policies pay actual cash value (after depreciation) first, then release the withheld depreciation once repairs or replacement are completed. Missing the deadline to claim that recoverable depreciation is a common way homeowners lose money.

If you only take one piece of fire damage insurance claim help from this article, make it this: photograph first, clean second.

Building a Complete Contents Inventory

The contents inventory is where most fire claims come up short, simply because people cannot remember everything they owned. Work room by room, and inside each room work drawer by drawer and shelf by shelf. For each item list the description, quantity, approximate age, where it was bought if known, and a current replacement price.

Helpful sources for rebuilding the list include online shopping accounts, credit card statements, phone photo libraries, social media pictures from holidays and birthdays, and warranty registrations. Do not forget items people routinely overlook: pantry food, cleaning supplies, linens, holiday decorations, tools, garage contents and items in attic storage.

Getting Fire Damage Insurance Claim Help From a Public Adjuster

Your insurance company will send its own adjuster, whose job is to evaluate the claim on the insurer's behalf. A licensed public adjuster works for you instead. In Texas, public adjusters are licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI), and you can verify any adjuster's license on the TDI website before signing anything.

On a fire loss, a public adjuster can help by:

  • Preparing a detailed, line-item repair estimate that includes smoke-affected areas outside the fire room.
  • Building and pricing the contents inventory.
  • Tracking ALE and making sure Loss of Use submissions are complete.
  • Identifying code upgrade, debris removal and recoverable depreciation amounts.
  • Handling communication with the carrier so you can focus on your family.

Anyone offering fire damage insurance claim help should be willing to show you their license and explain their fee in writing up front. Fire claims are complex, and the right help depends on the size of the loss. Our Galveston fire claims page explains how we handle these files locally.

Common Mistakes That Shrink Fire Settlements

  • Accepting the first estimate without review. Initial estimates sometimes omit items like cleaning of unburned rooms, HVAC duct replacement, insulation or electrical inspection.
  • Letting a contractor dictate scope before the claim is settled. Get the scope agreed in writing before work starts.
  • Giving recorded statements without preparation. Stick to facts you know. It is fine to say you do not know.
  • Missing proof of loss deadlines. If your insurer requests a sworn proof of loss, note the due date and submit it on time.
  • Discarding damaged items too early. Photograph, list and get written permission first.

How Long Does a Fire Claim Take in Texas?

Timelines vary with the size and complexity of the loss. Texas does set expectations for insurers through the Prompt Payment of Claims Act in Chapter 542 of the Texas Insurance Code, which includes deadlines for acknowledging claims, requesting information, and accepting or rejecting them. If your claim seems stalled, ask your carrier in writing what information they still need and when they expect to make a decision. Keep copies of everything you send.

Your Fire Claim Checklist

  • Fire department incident report requested
  • Claim number and adjuster contact recorded
  • Property secured and receipts saved
  • ALE limits confirmed and receipts organized
  • Room-by-room photos and video completed
  • Contents inventory started
  • Policy declarations page and full policy obtained
  • Replacement cost vs. actual cash value confirmed
  • Code upgrade and debris removal coverage checked

faq.q: How soon should I report a house fire to my insurance company?
faq.a: As soon as possible. Most policies require prompt notice, and reporting quickly lets you start Additional Living Expense coverage and get an adjuster assigned. Write down your claim number and the name of everyone you speak with.

faq.q: Does homeowners insurance cover smoke damage in rooms that did not burn?
faq.a: Smoke and soot damage to other areas of the home is generally part of a covered fire loss under most homeowners policies, but it is often underestimated. Document soot in closets, cabinets, ceilings and HVAC vents so those areas are included in the estimate.

faq.q: Can a public adjuster help with a fire claim that is already open?
faq.a: Yes. A licensed Texas public adjuster can step in at any stage of an open claim, including after you receive the insurer's first estimate. They will review the policy, re-inspect the loss and prepare their own documentation to support the claim.
